title: Outlook MCP Server Setup for AI Agents (2026)
summary: Outlook MCP servers let AI applications access Outlook mail and calendar. Configure yours by understanding constraints and common troubleshooting steps.
body_markdown:
## When to use Activepieces alongside an Outlook MCP server


Use Activepieces when the work should happen without anyone typing a prompt. A restarted client fixes an MCP session, but a job that must fire at 7am has no client to restart.


Ask a question in an AI client and an MCP server answers: it calls Graph with your token, and it stops. Nothing runs while you're away. Four jobs fit that badly and work better as a workflow:


- Filing new mail into a sheet
- Daily calendar digests
- Alerts on mail from a particular sender
- Scheduled attachment saving


Each is a trigger plus a fixed action, so a model deciding what to do on every run adds cost and failure modes for no gain.


### Official Microsoft server or a community one


For this decision, the choice doesn't matter. Activepieces has its own Outlook connector, one of the 741 integrations counted in its open source monorepo, so a workflow doesn't depend on whichever MCP server you picked.


It can also expose a workflow as an MCP tool. Your client then calls "save this week's attachments" instead of getting open-ended mailbox access, which keeps the scope your admin approved smaller.


### Prerequisites for an Outlook MCP server


Nothing in Activepieces is required to get an Outlook MCP server working. Fix consent and tokens first, since those failures happen before any automation layer is involved.


Once the Outlook integration is connected, an agent can call it: the action that runs as a step in your flow is also a tool schema on the project's MCP server, so Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor reach the Graph permissions you already consented to.


Nothing gets exported or wired up a second time, and that matters because a catalog you have to re-integrate for your agents is a second migration.


The Integrations Framework and MCP Server docs describe it, and packages/integrations in the MIT-licensed open source repo shows one integration action behind both uses.


Once that works, the cost question is short.


The pricing below, as listed on the[Activepieces pricing page](https://www.activepieces.com/pricing) in October 2026, shows a steep step at the top, and the first two tiers are where most single-mailbox automations will be tried, which means you'll face a significant cost jump when you try to scale.


At 0 $ per month, Free lets you build the sender alert and see whether it earns its keep before paying anything. Plus is 20 $ per month, cheap enough to run on one person's budget without a purchasing conversation.


Team is 200 $ per month, ten times Plus, which only makes sense once several people share the workflows.


Start on Free with one trigger, one action, and the narrowest Graph scope that covers it.
